context_text: GWAS analyses of 439 serum proteins (mapped to one UniProt ID) or protein groups (mapped to multiple UniProt IDs) levels were conducted using data from 15,035 participants from Generation Scotland. We observed 199,489 genome-wide significant (P < 1.2 × 10^(−10)) SNP associations with 398 (91%) of the proteins/protein groups. Following conditional analysis, 1553 independent signals were identified with the lead variant defined as the SNP with the lowest P-value within the given locus (Supplementary Data 1). 1199 of the significant pQTLs were found in uniquely mapped proteins (i.e, non-protein groups), 656 (54.7%) of which were cis (±1 Mb), and 543 (45.3%) trans (Fig. 1A). Over 40% of discovered pQTLs (404 cis and 200 trans) were associated with a single protein. Our results also indicated the presence of a pQTL hotspot within SERPINA1, with 17 independent signals generating 181 associations with 140 proteins. 71 proteins/protein groups had only one independent pQTL whilst 48 protein/protein groups had seven or more (Fig. 1B). When comparing effect size with minor allele frequency, a negative correlation (for cis loci: r_(Pearson) = −0.60, P = 1.0 × 10^(−64); for trans loci: r_(Pearson) = −0.72, P = 3.6 × 10^(−88)) between the log beta and the log MAF was observed (Fig. 1C). In general, for the same MAF, larger effect sizes were found with cis loci than with trans (Fig. 1C). An inverse association (r_(Pearson) = −0.15, P = 1.8 × 10^(−4)) was found between strength of cis pQTL and distance from transcription start site (Fig. 1D). The pQTL analysis was repeated to include a SNP-sex interaction term to test for sex differences in genetic effects. One significant association (P < 1.2 × 10^(−10)) was found: a cis locus in Ceruloplasmin (CP) (Supplementary Data 2). This locus remained significant after running a sensitivity analysis which included contraception as a covariate to determine if the signal was being driven by hormonal contraceptive use.

context_text: The significant pQTLs discovered in our study were compared to three previous proteomics GWAS. These include two large-scale affinity-based proteomics GWAS using Olink Explore 3072 PEA in the UK Biobank^(11) and SomaScan v4 in the deCODE study^(10), and a smaller-scale mass-spectrometry proteomics GWAS using the MS-based Seer Proteograph platform in the Tarkin study^(18). For all significant pQTLs in the current study, we performed lookup analyses in these studies, where the same protein was assessed and also demonstrated significant associations. We replicated 46 of 199 (23.12%), 64 of 275 (23.27%) and 10 of 25 (40%) pQTLs with the Sun et al.^(11), Eldjarn et al.^(10), and Suhre et al.^(18), studies, respectively (see Table 1). Effect sizes of the overlapping associations correlated highly between platforms (R_(Pearson) = 0.94 (MS:UKB^(11))); 0.90 (MS:deCODE cohort^(10)); 0.89 (MS:Tarkin^(18)) (Fig. 2). A list of the overlapping proteins-SNP associations can be found in Supplementary Data 3, 4 and 5.

context_text: Identifying causal protein—disease pathways could aid the discovery of novel drug targets; human genetic evidence increases the success rate for approval of developed drugs^(22,23). Given this, we tested whether any of the proteins or protein groups were causally associated with 79 disease or health outcomes (for full list see Supplementary Data 6). We identified 13 proteins that were putatively causal factors for 17 traits (Supplementary Data 7), giving a total of 31 significant results (inverse variance weighted (IVW) method with P < 1.59 × 10^(−6), at least one other method with P < 0.05 and a minimum of 3 SNP instruments). The causal direction was from exposure (protein) to disease outcome, as determined by the Steiger directionality test. The proteins apolipoprotein E (APOE) and apolipoprotein B (APOB) were each associated with five of the cardiovascular-related and metabolic traits (Fig. 3). The strongest APOE association was with systolic blood pressure (IVW beta = 0.42, P = 8.5 × 10^(−16)) while the strongest APOB association was with LDL cholesterol (IVW beta = 1.17, P = 1.4 × 10^(−39)). This was supported by posterior probabilities of >0.99 (H4) for both LDL and HDL cholesterol in colocalization analysis, suggesting a shared causal variant. Significant MR results were also found for three neuropsychiatric traits: autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The trypsin inhibitors inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor heavy chain 3 (ITIH3) and inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor heavy chain 4 (ITIH4) were associated with Schizophrenia (IVW log odds = −0.16, P = 1.7 × 10^(−9)) and ASD (IVW log odds = −0.21, P = 6.3 × 10^(−7)), respectively. Alpha-1-Antitrypsin (AAT) was also found to be associated with ASD (IVW log odds = −0.11, P = 4.2 × 10^(−7)). AAT, ITIH3 and ITIH4 were also found to have associations or interactions with each other as defined by StringDB^(24) (Supplementary Fig. 1). One protein, Immunoglobulin heavy constant mu (IGHM), showed evidence for a causal association with Alzheimer’s Disease (IVW log odds = −0.063, P = 4.3 × 10^(−7)) (Fig. 4). To further support our findings of causal associations between our protein exposures and disease outcomes we ran colocalisation analysis using coloc. 15 out of the 31 (48.4%) significant MR results showed strong evidence (PP.H4.abf>0.8), with a further two (6.5%) showing moderate evidence (PP.H4.abf>0.6) of a shared causal variant between the exposure and outcome (Supplementary Data 7).

context_text: 439 proteins and protein groups were considered; 133 (30.3%) of these were uniquely mapped to one UniProt ID (termed “proteins”), with the remaining 306 (69.7%) mapping to multiple potential UniProt IDs (termed “protein groups”). 199 of these protein groups represent different isoforms of the same protein, and 107 mixed protein groups where the signal mapped to different proteins. 138 out of the 199 isoform signals were mapped to proteins that were identified more than once (repeated isoform groups). We use a “GX” naming system, where “G” signifies a group and “X” refers to a number to identify these repeated isoform groups (Table 2). For example, Apolipoprotein D was identified twice, with one of the signals annotating to three isoforms [UniProt identifiers: P05090, C9JF17, C9JX71] and was given the name Apolipoprotein D (G1) and another signal mapped to two isoforms [UniProt identifiers: P05090.C9JF17], therefore was named Apolipoprotein D (G2). 61 signals were annotated to protein isoform groups that did not repeat; these therefore only have a “G” after their protein name. We used a “PG X” naming system to identify the 107 signals that map to multiple different proteins. For example, one signal is annotated to multiple immunoglobulins (Immunoglobulin lambda variable 3-27, Immunoglobulin lambda variable 3-25 and Immunoglobulin lambda variable 3-16), and therefore is referred to as protein group 1 (PG 1). As can be observed with the PG1 example, in many cases, the protein groups with mixed labels contain related proteins. In some instances, a protein is identified as a unique signal and as several protein groups. For example, one mass spectrometry signal mapped to Alpha-1-antitrypsin identified via a single UniProt ID P01009; therefore, it was named Alpha-1-antitrypsin. However, five other mass spectrometry signals mapped to five different combinations of UniProt IDs that were all related to Alpha-1-antitrypsin and were therefore named Alpha-1-antitrypsin G1 to G5. Given that these groups originate from different signals, they were maintained as separate entities in downstream analysis. Annotation of the 439 proteins considered in this study is provided in Supplementary Data 11.

context_text: GWAS were used to identify pQTLs for protein levels (N = 15,035, Fig. 5A). Linear regression was run using the fastGWA command in GCTA (version 1.94.1)^(71). Protein levels were transformed by rank-based inverse normalisation. Age, sex and 20 genetic principal components (to capture population structure) were included as fixed effect covariates in the GWAS models. Correlations between all protein levels and covariates are detailed in Supplementary Data 12. A sparse genetic relationship matrix (GRM) was generated using a GRM cut-off value of 0.05 and fitted as a random effect to control for family structure. A Bonferroni statistical significance threshold was set at P < 1.2 × 10^(−10) (genome-wide significance threshold divided by number of inferred proteins, 5 × 10^(−8)/439). Cis pQTLs were defined as variants lying within 1 Mb of the transcription start site for the gene encoding the primary protein target. Lead-independent pQTLs were identified via conditional and joint analysis of the summary statistics for each protein using GCTA-COJO^(71,72). Default settings were specified, which included a stepwise selection procedure across 10 Mb regions and SNP linkage disequilibrium (LD) cut-offs set to R^(2) < 0.9 to avoid multicollinearity. The statistical significance threshold was once again set to P < 1.2 × 10^(−10). HRC^(64) imputed data from Generation Scotland was used as the reference panel for LD calculations.

Age, sex and the first 20 genetic principal components were included as covariates. B MR: two-sample Mendelian randomisation was carried out using results from our protein GWAS and summary statistics for GWAS of the 79 selected disease outcomes. MR was run for the 398 proteins with pQTLs in the GWAS results. Figure created with BioRender.com.

context_text: To investigate possible causal associations between protein levels and disease risk, two-sample MR^(76) analyses were carried out using TwoSampleMR (version 0.6.8) for each protein with >1 independent pQTL (exposure, n = 398) and a list of 78 common causes of morbidity and mortality taken from Gudjonsson et al.^(77), plus critical COVID^(78) as outcomes (Fig. 4B). A full list of these outcomes can be found in Supplementary Data 6, along with source information for the summary statistics. The lead independent SNPs were included as instruments for each protein and inverse-variance weighted (IVW) MR was run alongside MR-Egger, weighted median MR, weighted mode MR and simple mode MR sensitivity analyses. Evidence of directional horizontal pleiotropy was queried for by testing for a non-zero Egger MR regression intercept. MR Steiger directionality^(79) was used to determine the causal direction of the instruments on the exposure and outcome. A Bonferroni statistical significance threshold was set at P < 1.59 × 10^(−6) (0.05/(number of outcomes x number of exposures)). An MR result was considered significant if the IVW p-value was below this threshold, at least one other method had P < 0.05, and it had at least 3 SNP instruments.

segments.text: To investigate possible causal associations between protein levels and disease risk, two-sample MR^(76) analyses were carried out using TwoSampleMR (version 0.6.8) for each protein with >1 independent pQTL (exposure, n = 398) and a list of 78 common causes of morbidity and mortality taken from Gudjonsson et al.^(77), plus critical COVID^(78) as outcomes (Fig. 4B). A full list of these outcomes can be found in Supplementary Data 6, along with source information for the summary statistics. The lead independent SNPs were included as instruments for each protein and inverse-variance weighted (IVW) MR was run alongside MR-Egger, weighted median MR, weighted mode MR and simple mode MR sensitivity analyses. Evidence of directional horizontal pleiotropy was queried for by testing for a non-zero Egger MR regression intercept. MR Steiger directionality^(79) was used to determine the causal direction of the instruments on the exposure and outcome. A Bonferroni statistical significance threshold was set at P < 1.59 × 10^(−6) (0.05/(number of outcomes x number of exposures)). An MR result was considered significant if the IVW p-value was below this threshold, at least one other method had P < 0.05, and it had at least 3 SNP instruments.
